Empirical Research Plan  

------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Cohort-by-District Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS).

•  First stage (schooling): exploit two dimensions of plausibly exogenous variation—  
  a) cross-district intensity of construction (more schools built per 1,000 children in districts with low 1972 enrolment) and  
  b) differential exposure across birth cohorts (children <12 in 1974 could still benefit; older cohorts could not).  
  This is a “dose” DID with continuous treatment (number of schools per 1,000 children).

•  Second stage (wages): use the DID-generated variation in education as an instrument for completed years of schooling to estimate the causal return to schooling.

The DID structure absorbs district fixed effects (capturing time-invariant district traits) and cohort fixed effects (capturing national time shocks). Exogeneity comes from the mechanical allocation formula, making the program intensity orthogonal to unobserved district trends once pre-program enrolment is controlled for.

------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
SCHOOL_EXPOSURE_idc = (number of SD schools built 1973-79 in birth district d per 1,000 children aged 5-14 in 1971) × Exposure_c,  
where Exposure_c = max(0, 12 – Age_in_1974). This yields the potential number of additional school slots per child that cohort c could exploit.

Control group  
Older cohorts with Exposure_c = 0 (i.e., born ≤1962, age ≥12 in 1974) living in all districts provide counterfactual trends.

Treatment timing  
Program starts in school year 1973/74; schools are largely in place by 1978/79.

------------------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel Cohort Trends: In the absence of school construction, differences in schooling outcomes across successive cohorts would have evolved similarly across districts with different planned school intensity.  
Plausibility: allocation rule tied to pre-program enrolment, not to trends; we can check using pre-1973 cohorts.

A2. Exogenous Allocation Conditional on Pre-Program Enrolment: Conditional on 1972 enrolment and other pre-program covariates, number of schools built is uncorrelated with unobserved determinants of future schooling and wages.  
Plausibility: central-government formula reduces local political discretion.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment (no spillovers across districts): Children seldom cross district boundaries for primary school; district-of-birth captures exposure.  
Plausibility: Indonesian primary schools draw very locally; we will test sensitivity to excluding migrants.

A4. No Selective Migration by Unborn or Very Young Children: Parents did not migrate anticipating district-level school construction.  
Plausibility: short program roll-out horizon; we can compare migration propensities across birth cohorts.

A5. Relevance: School construction must increase schooling; testable in first stage.

------------------------------------------------------------  
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  

T1. Internal Migration.  
  •  Strategy: (i) restrict to individuals living in their birth district in 1995; (ii) show results robust when using district of birth only (IFLS provides migration history).

T2. Concurrent Water/Sanitation Program.  
  •  Strategy: control for water-program intensity × exposure; run falsification test on pre-program adult height or other outcomes the school program should not affect.

T3. Differential Grade Repetition or School Quality.  
  •  Strategy: use IFLS grade-repetition data to show repetition not mechanically driving years of schooling; include district-specific linear cohort trends as robustness.

------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# --------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed effects
library(sandwich)    # robust vcov
library(lmtest)      # coeftest

# --------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
supas <- fread("supas_1995_males_1950_1972.csv")      # individual data
sd    <- fread("sd_construction_1973_1979.csv")       # schools built
pop71 <- fread("census1971_children.csv")             # child pop 5-14

# --------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Construct Variables
# a) schools per 1,000 children
sd <- merge(sd, pop71, by = "district_id")
sd[, schools_per1000 := schools_built / children_5_14 * 1000]

# b) attach to individuals by district of birth
supas <- merge(supas, sd[, .(district_id, schools_per1000)], by = "district_id")

# c) exposure of cohort
supas[, age_1974 := 1974 - birth_year]
supas[, exposure := pmax(0, 12 - age_1974)]          # 0–12
supas[, treat_intensity := schools_per1000 * exposure]

# d) controls
supas[, yob_fe := factor(birth_year)]
supas[, district_fe := factor(district_id)]

# e) outcome variables
supas[, ln_wage := log(hourly_wage)]                 # keep only wage earners

# --------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main First-Stage Regression (schooling)
fs <- feols(education_years ~ treat_intensity | yob_fe + district_fe, 
            data = supas, cluster = ~district_id)
summary(fs)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 4. Second Stage (returns to schooling)
iv <- feols(ln_wage ~ 1 | yob_fe + district_fe | education_years ~ treat_intensity, 
            data = supas[!is.na(ln_wage)], cluster = ~district_id)
summary(iv)

# --------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: add district-specific linear cohort trends
supas[, district_trend := birth_year * as.numeric(district_fe)]

fs_rb <- feols(education_years ~ treat_intensity | yob_fe + district_fe + district_trend,
               data = supas, cluster = ~district_id)
summary(fs_rb)
```

------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results  

•  First stage: an additional primary school per 1,000 children accessible throughout the full 6 grades (exposure = 6) should raise completed schooling by roughly 0.15–0.20 years.  
•  Returns: classic Mincerian estimates in developing countries cluster around 7–10 % per additional year. Given Indonesia’s labour market, I expect ≈ 8 % increase in hourly wages per extra year of schooling induced by the program.

------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/IV)  
C1: Pre-trends verified in placebo cohorts → 1  
C2: Exogeneity of treatment given allocation rule → 1  
C3: No anticipation/partial treatment of older cohorts → 1  
C4: No spillovers/migration bias → 0.5 (some concern)  
C5: Robustness to alternative specifications & controls → 1  

Total: 4.5 / 5.
